title: Systemic Autoimmune Disease: SLE, Rheumatoid Arthritis & Immunosuppression Safety
html:
Systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases result from immune activity directed against the body's own tissues. The illness and its treatment can affect joints, skin, kidneys, blood cells, lungs, heart, nervous system, fertility, infection risk, and daily function. The RN must recognize patterns rather than diagnose from one antibody test, distinguish possible disease activity from infection or medication toxicity, detect organ-threatening change, and make a complex treatment plan safe and usable.

Learning goals

  • Compare systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) without relying on one symptom or laboratory result.
  • Recognize possible lupus nephritis, serositis, neurologic disease, vasculitis, inflammatory lung disease, and cervical-spine risk.
  • Evaluate fever and deterioration for infection, flare, thrombosis, and medication toxicity at the same time.
  • Monitor hydroxychloroquine, glucocorticoids, methotrexate, conventional DMARDs, and biologic or targeted therapy safely.
  • Support vaccination, reproductive planning, joint protection, activity, sun protection, and shared decision-making.

Autoimmune disease is a pattern, not a positive antibody

SLE can affect multiple organs in different combinations and over time. Possible features include fatigue, fever, photosensitive rash, oral or nasal ulcers, inflammatory joint symptoms, hair loss, Raynaud phenomenon, cytopenias, serositis, kidney disease, neurologic symptoms, and thrombosis. RA primarily causes chronic inflammatory synovitis, often involving small joints symmetrically, but may also affect lungs, eyes, blood vessels, nerves, bone, and cardiovascular risk.

No single symptom or laboratory result proves either disease. Antinuclear antibodies can support SLE evaluation but are not specific enough to diagnose SLE alone. Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies can support RA assessment, but seronegative disease exists and positive tests can occur without active RA. Combine history, physical findings, urine and blood trends, imaging, classification criteria used by qualified clinicians, and sometimes biopsy.

Distinguish inflammatory joint disease from mechanical pain

Ask which joints are affected, whether swelling is present, how long morning stiffness lasts, whether symptoms improve or worsen with movement, and how function has changed. Inspect and gently assess tenderness, warmth, swelling, range of motion, grip, gait, deformity, skin, and assistive-device use. Inflammatory arthritis often produces prolonged morning stiffness and objective synovitis; mechanical pain more often worsens with use and has shorter stiffness, but patterns overlap.

Do not force painful joints through range of motion during active inflammation. Balance rest during acute symptoms with prescribed range of motion, strengthening, aerobic activity, energy conservation, heat or cold according to response, occupational strategies, and fall prevention. Early disease-modifying therapy is important in RA because pain relief alone does not prevent structural joint damage. Track function and disease activity rather than relying only on a pain score or inflammatory marker.

SLE: screen every system and trend change from baseline

Ask about new rash or sun exposure, ulcers, pleuritic or positional chest pain, dyspnea, edema, foamy or dark urine, reduced urine output, headache, seizure, confusion, focal weakness, bruising, pregnancy possibility, and medication adherence. Assess temperature, blood pressure, oxygenation, cardiopulmonary findings, neurologic status, joints, skin, weight, edema, and urine trend. Review blood counts, creatinine, urinalysis and quantified urine protein, liver tests, and ordered immune markers in context.

Complement and anti-double-stranded DNA trends may help the specialist assess disease activity in some patients, but they do not replace the clinical picture. A normal value does not make new organ symptoms harmless, and an abnormal value alone does not prove that fever is a flare. Treatment targets remission or low disease activity while minimizing organ damage and medication toxicity.

Lupus nephritis can be quiet before kidney function falls

New proteinuria, hematuria, cellular casts, hypertension, edema, weight gain, or reduced urine output raises concern for lupus nephritis. Creatinine may remain near baseline early, so do not wait for advanced kidney failure before reporting urine changes. Confirm specimen quality, quantify ordered protein loss, trend blood pressure and kidney function, assess volume status and potassium, and involve rheumatology and nephrology promptly.

Kidney biopsy may identify the histologic pattern and guide therapy. Follow the pre- and post-biopsy bleeding assessment described in Lesson 86. Escalate rapidly rising creatinine, pulmonary edema, severe hypertension, hyperkalemia, or oliguria. New hemoptysis or hypoxemia with kidney findings may signal a pulmonary–renal emergency and requires immediate respiratory support and specialist evaluation.

Cardiopulmonary, neurologic, and vascular red flags

Pleuritic chest pain may reflect pleuritis, infection, or pulmonary embolism; positional pain can occur with pericarditis; dyspnea can reflect infection, interstitial lung disease, pulmonary hypertension, effusion, anemia, thrombosis, heart disease, or medication toxicity. Hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds, worsening dyspnea, or pulsus findings can signal tamponade physiology and require emergency escalation rather than routine pain treatment.

Seizure, psychosis, acute confusion, focal deficit, severe headache, or vision change requires emergency neurologic evaluation; do not assume it is “lupus brain.” Consider stroke, infection, metabolic disturbance, hypertension, medication effect, and thrombosis. Patients with antiphospholipid antibodies may have increased thrombotic or pregnancy risk, but laboratory positivity alone does not establish the full syndrome or authorize anticoagulation.

RA can involve the cervical spine, especially in established erosive disease. New neck or occipital pain, limb weakness or numbness, gait change, bowel or bladder symptoms, or signs of cord compression require urgent evaluation. Before surgery, intubation, or forceful neck positioning, communicate known cervical disease and symptoms; maintain neutral alignment as directed and do not perform aggressive neck manipulation.

Flare, infection, or both?

Fever, fatigue, cytopenias, joint symptoms, and inflammatory-marker changes can occur with active autoimmune disease, infection, or medication toxicity. Immunosuppressive therapy may blunt fever and inflammatory signs. Assess hemodynamics, oxygenation, mental status, focal symptoms, exposure, lines or wounds, neutrophil count, organ function, recent therapy, and cultures or imaging as ordered. Treat instability and follow sepsis or infection protocols without waiting for a flare diagnosis.

Do not independently increase corticosteroids for undifferentiated fever or abruptly stop all immune therapy. The treating team balances infection control, adrenal risk, and the danger of rebound disease. Communicate the exact medication, dose, timing, recent changes, and last biologic infusion or injection. A patient can have infection and autoimmune activity simultaneously.

Hydroxychloroquine and glucocorticoid safety

Current SLE guidance supports hydroxychloroquine for most patients unless contraindicated, with individualized dosing and toxicity monitoring. Verify baseline and ongoing eye-screening plans and teach patients to report new visual change. Review kidney function, interacting medicines, cardiac history, and the actual product and dose. Hydroxychloroquine prevents disease activity over time; it is not a rescue medicine for an acute organ emergency.

Glucocorticoids can rapidly suppress inflammation but can also cause infection, hyperglycemia, hypertension, mood or sleep change, osteoporosis, muscle weakness, eye disease, skin fragility, and adrenal suppression. Current strategies emphasize minimizing exposure while maintaining disease control. Monitor dose and duration, glucose, blood pressure, infection, bone protection, function, and taper instructions. Long-term systemic therapy should not be stopped abruptly unless the prescriber directs a safe plan.

Methotrexate, DMARDs, biologics, and targeted therapy

For nononcologic rheumatic disease, methotrexate is usually taken once weekly, not daily. Verify the exact day, dose, route, folic-acid plan, pregnancy status or reproductive plan, blood counts, liver and kidney function, alcohol use, interactions, and symptoms of infection, mouth ulcers, bruising, dyspnea, or cough. A daily-versus-weekly error can cause severe marrow, mucosal, hepatic, and other toxicity.

Other conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), biologics, and targeted medicines have agent-specific risks. Before selected therapies, clinicians may screen for tuberculosis, hepatitis B or C, pregnancy, malignancy history, heart failure, demyelinating disease, and baseline blood or organ function. During treatment, monitor infection, cytopenias, liver or kidney injury, infusion or injection reactions, thrombosis, cardiovascular events, and other product-specific effects. Do not combine or hold therapies based on class name alone; use the current rheumatology plan.

Vaccination, pregnancy, and daily self-management

Review vaccination before significant immunosuppression when feasible. Non-live vaccines are generally safe in altered immunocompetence, although immune response and timing may differ. Live vaccines may be unsafe during substantial immunosuppression and require clinician review. Never advise a patient to stop a DMARD or biologic solely to receive a vaccine without the disease- and drug-specific plan.

Discuss pregnancy intentions early because disease activity and medication safety affect pregnancy, and pregnancy affects treatment choices. Some medicines are compatible while others can cause fetal harm; do not stop every medicine automatically or rely on a label remembered from another drug. Coordinate rheumatology and obstetric expertise and use reliable contraception when required by the prescribed therapy.

Teach sun protection for photosensitive lupus, smoking cessation, cardiovascular risk reduction, infection precautions, oral and skin care, bone health, balanced activity, joint protection, sleep and mental-health support, and keeping an updated medication list. Encourage the patient to report fever, breathing difficulty, chest pain, neurologic change, reduced urine, rapid edema, severe weakness, unusual bleeding, pregnancy, or a new vision change promptly.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify the diagnosed disease, baseline organ involvement, joint and skin findings, urine and kidney trends, cardiopulmonary or neurologic symptoms, fever, medication schedule, and immune status.
  2. Analyze cues: Compare infection, flare, thrombosis, medication toxicity, and unrelated disease; connect laboratory changes with symptoms rather than treating an antibody or inflammatory marker alone.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Sepsis, respiratory failure, pulmonary hemorrhage, tamponade, stroke or seizure, rapidly progressive nephritis, cord compression, and severe drug toxicity outrank routine symptom management.
  4. Generate solutions: Activate emergency and specialty pathways, obtain ordered cultures and organ studies, protect airway and perfusion, reconcile immunosuppressants, and prepare disease-specific treatment.
  5. Take action: Escalate exact changes, administer authorized therapy, protect joints and skin, monitor high-risk medicines, preserve neutral neck alignment when indicated, and coordinate vaccination and reproductive care.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Confirm improving function and disease activity, stable organ function, controlled infection, safe medication monitoring, prevention of damage, and patient understanding of warning signs and follow-up.

Clinical example

A patient with SLE taking prednisone and mycophenolate develops fever, cough, fatigue, and worsening joint pain. The RN does not assume a lupus flare. The RN assesses airway, oxygenation, hemodynamics, mental status, lung findings, urine output, rash and joints; reviews immunosuppressant timing and laboratory trends; follows the infection and sepsis pathway; obtains ordered cultures and imaging; and urgently communicates the possibility of infection, flare, or both. Steroid and immunosuppressant changes are made by the treating team with attention to adrenal suppression and organ disease.
